title: 50 Years of the Institute of Adult Education: A Nation’s Promise, Renewed
summary: A reflection on the Institute of Adult Education’s Golden Jubilee and the national commitments shaping the future of lifelong learning in Tanzania.

author.name: Joseph Masonda
author.role: Communications Officer | Digital Marketer | Website Designer | Content Creator | AI Enthusiast | Framer Developer | Writer

content.text: When Tanzania gained independence, the country faced significant challenges. In the years that followed, the nation’s founding father, Mwalimu Julius Nyerere, recognised a stark reality: 75 per cent of Tanzanians were unable to read or write. This inspired a vision in which education would become a foundation for national development and self-reliance.

Nyerere stressed that government spending on education must equip Tanganyikans with skills and knowledge needed for development, insisting that adults must be educated because their attitudes have an immediate impact. From this vision sprang one of the most impactful movements in Tanzania’s post-independence history: the Institute of Adult Education.

When we got our independence, our first President, Mwalimu Julius Nyerere, recognized three major enemies: poverty, disease, and ignorance. To defeat ignorance, he launched the national campaign against illiteracy, which made Tanzania one of the most successful developing countries in eradicating illiteracy.
content.attribution: Prof. Adolf Mkenda, Minister of Education, Science and Technology

content.text: Today, Nyerere’s dream remains a vital part of the country’s development journey. From 25–27 August 2025, leaders, practitioners and partners gathered at the Julius Nyerere International Convention Centre to mark the Golden Jubilee of Tanzania’s Institute of Adult Education (IAE), under the theme “Lifelong Learning for Sustainable Development”.
It was more than a ceremony; it was a recommitment to a national movement that began half a century ago and now looks confidently to the next.
Adult Education is no longer just about reading, writing and numeracy. It has gone far beyond that; it is now a driver of economic, social and technological development in Tanzania.
A partnership that shapes systems, not just projects

IAE offers ongoing education, research and training opportunities for adult learners, serving as a vital institution for second chances and new beginnings. Over the past 50 years, it has worked alongside the Directorate of Adult Education and local committees, contributing to important improvements in literacy rates.
Why this milestone matters for Tanzania

The anniversary mattered because the stakes are national. Adult and non-formal education can raise incomes, expand entrepreneurship, improve public health and deepen civic participation. The Prime Minister’s address linked policy with lived experience, including local innovation, women adding value to agricultural produce, and home-grown manufacturing skills taught and applied through adult education pathways.
In short, the major task of this Institute is to oversee the implementation of the government’s vision that ‘no Tanzanian is left behind’ in accessing the right and opportunity to education.

The Minister of Education also highlighted that IAE now has a more important role than ever before. The Institute has been at the forefront of adapting modern skills, training adult education administrators, and undertaking research that improves accessibility for all groups. Lifelong learning means that even people who can read and write can still benefit from continuing to educate themselves.

items: Alternative pathways: MoEST to issue a policy circular guiding primary and secondary school leavers who cannot proceed in the formal system toward credible alternative education routes.
A Community Learning Centre in every ward: MoEST to require CLCs nationwide to ensure equitable, local access to learning opportunities.

Governance and oversight: review and modernise Adult Education Committee guidelines from national to ward level, clarifying leadership, composition and roles and aligning them with current socio-economic contexts.
A dedicated department: establish a Department of Adult Education at all levels of implementation.
Expand lifelong learning opportunities for all citizens.
Harness innovation and technology to improve access and quality.
Ensure governance structures and policies keep pace with Tanzania’s socio-economic changes.

content.text: The 50th Anniversary of the Institute of Adult Education reaffirmed Tanzania’s vision for inclusive lifelong learning. With strong government leadership, IAE’s institutional mandate and the commitment of partners, the next 50 years can bring even greater achievements in adult education and lifelong learning for sustainable national development.
